```{r}
#| include: false

## Hormone Dataset
library(jtools)
library(psych)
library(gplots)
library(ggplot2)
d <- read.csv("https://www.dropbox.com/scl/fi/97h771dt55vum5lhpf9ng/haas_hormone_dataset.csv?rlkey=sc5rvwdmtjn5inuqm1xok5bwd&dl=1", stringsAsFactors = T)

d$age[d$age < 0] <- NA
d$sexF <- as.factor(d$sex)
levels(d$sexF) <- c("Male", "Female")
d$sexF <- relevel(d$sexF, ref = "Female")
plot(d$sexF)
summary(d$sexF)
```

## [Check-In (No R Needed)](https://forms.gle/gaKpikRoyqANKQDr9)

**(Click through the tabs to see the linear models.)**

::::::::: panel-tabset
#### Dataset

These data come from a study of Haas business students; we'll focus on the following variables.

- **narc_scale :** a likert scale measure of narcissism - how self-interested the person is (higher scores = the person was higher in narcissism)
- **sex :** the person's biological sex, measured as a categorical variable with two levels (M = Male; F = Female)
- **test_mean :** the person's average of two separate testosterone samples.

#### M1. {.smaller}

::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
#| fig-height: 5
#| fig-width: 5

mod1 <- lm(narc_scale ~ sexF, data = d)
plotmeans(narc_scale ~ sexF, data = d, connect = F, xlab = "Sex", ylab = "Narcissism (Scale)")
```
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
export_summs(mod1, error_pos = "right",
             coefs = c("Intercept" = "(Intercept)",
                       "Sex (Male)" = "sexFMale"), digits = 3)
```
:::
:::::

#### M1 (b). {.smaller}

```{r}
#| fig-height: 5
#| fig-width: 5
par(mfrow = c(2,2))
plot(mod1)
```

#### M2. {.smaller}

::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
#| fig-height: 5
#| fig-width: 5


mod2 <- lm(narc_scale ~ test_mean, data = d)
plot(narc_scale ~ test_mean, data = d, xlab = "Testosterone", ylab = "Narcissism (Scale)")

```
:::

# PART 1 : When Models Get Complicated

### Multiple Regression {.smaller}

:::::::::::: panel-tabset
#### Model 1. {.smaller}

Sex is related to narcissism.

::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}

#### Model 3.

**How are they uniquely related?**

```{r}
mod3 <- lm(narc_scale ~ sexF + test_mean, data = d)
export_summs(mod1, mod2, mod3, error_format = "",  error_pos = "right", digits = 3,
             coefs = c("Testosterone" = "test_mean",
                       "Sex (Male)" = "sexFMale"))
```

#### Labeling Changes {.smaller}

1.  **"Independent" Effect.** The slope of the IV does not change when other variables are added to the model.
2.  **"Suppression" Effect.** The slope of the IV gets stronger (in either direction) when other variables are added to the model.
3.  "**Mediation" Effect.** The slope of the IV gets closer to zero when other variables are added to the model. *Careful : "mediation" often implies some causal relationship, and it is very hard (/impossible?) to estimate causal relationships without experimental methods. Some links in the weekly readings that go deeper into this.*

## PART 2 : Bootstrap Review

### The Code : a for-loop

1.  Questions about the code?
2.  What part of this code would you want to adapt to : estimate sampling error of the mean? estimate sampling error in $R^2$
3.  What are some other ways you could use a for-loop?

```{r}
#| eval: false

bucket <- array() # defines a space to save my work
for(i in c(1:1000)){ # repeating steps 1000 times & keeping track with i
  newfolk <- sample(1:nrow(d), nrow(d), replace = T) # new index of individuals; same sample size as original data, but wiht replacement
  newdata <- d[newfolk,] # new data, based on the new index
  modX <- lm(DV ~ IV, data = newdata) # new model, based on new data
  extrabucket[i] <- modX[2] # saving the slope (second term of the model)
}
```
